item.title: How Christian Premarital Counseling Can Save Your Marriage Before It Starts
item.description:
Using the SYMBIS Assessment to Build a Christ-Centered Foundation

Tom and Tina met at a gathering of mutual friends and quickly hit it off. After spending time in a group setting getting to know one another, Tom asked Tina out on their first date, and the rest is history. Tina believes Tom is “the one” because they have so much in common and have fun together – a perfect fit. Tom adores many qualities of Tina; she is beautiful, funny, and easy to be with.

They soon became engaged, and everything became focused on venues, menus, invitations, and preparations. So far, planning the wedding has been exciting and fun. They can’t wait to start their life together – it is going to be great.

Many couples spend months preparing for a wedding but little time preparing for marriage. By participating in Christian premarital counseling, couples will be guided to identify strengths, address challenges, develop tools, and gain insights. One of the most successful premarital tools available is the SYMBIS (Saving Your Marriage Before It Starts) Assessment developed by Drs. Les and Leslie Parrott.

Why Premarital Counseling Matters

According to research, couples who complete premarital counseling are 31% less likely to divorce and report higher marriage satisfaction. As couples are unique individuals created by God with their own stories from their family of origin, expectations and assumptions, family backgrounds, habits, and beliefs should be explored before the vows are exchanged. This will help to significantly improve marital outcomes.

Marriage is the uniting of two broken, sinful people in a fallen world. It takes work and intentionality to have a fulfilling and joyful union. As stated in Prov 24:3-4, “A house is built by wisdom, and it is established by understanding; by knowledge the rooms are filled with every precious and beautiful treasure.” (CSB)

Marriage is a sacred covenant and should not be entered lightly. According to the Cambridge Dictionary, “covenant” is defined as “a formal agreement or promise between two or more people.” A covenant is a lifelong binding, because as stated in Genesis 2:24, “two are united into one.” (NLT), thus, the importance of learning about one another before going down the aisle.

Exploring common areas of hidden conflict or expectations helps to promote a healthier union. The SYMBIS assessment areas include communication, conflict resolution, finances, roles and responsibilities, intimacy, spiritual life, and family relationships.

What is the SYMBIS assessment?

SYMBIS is a research-based premarital tool developed by Dr. Les and Leslie Parrott. It is specifically designed for engaged and seriously dating couples. The couples complete the assessment individually online, and then a report will be sent to their counselor to then go over in session. Personalized feedback is provided, along with identification of strengths and growth areas.

Areas Assessed by SYMBIS

Better Understanding of Personality styles assists couples in discovering habits that could create future conflict. By revealing blind spots, the assessment gives couples insight into potential challenges, allowing them to work together and better understand one another. God has created each one of us uniquely.

There are differences in sex (male/female), personality, and family background. These differences are what draw us together and complement one another. The assessment promotes growth individually and as a couple.

Search me, God, and know my heart.– Psalm 139:23

Improving communication by helping couples identify their communication strengths and weaknesses so that they learn how to hear and understand one another, thus encouraging healthy conversations about difficult topics and avoiding miscommunications.

Couples learn communication skills to help them listen with curiosity and reflect what they hear so their spouse will feel understood. Often, couples allow the busyness of life to affect their relationship. It is important to set aside time to meet and stay connected.

Can two walk together unless they are agreed? – Amos 3:3

Learning to navigate conflict by developing skills to work through challenging issues. It is not a matter of if conflict will occur but when. Even issues that seem small or inconsequential to one may be important, or an unmet need, to the other and, if left undiscussed, can lead to larger issues. Undiscussed issues can build up, causing couples to get defensive, shut down (stonewall), or respond poorly, so it is imperative to learn and use skills to resolve conflict.

Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry.– James 1:19

Understanding financial attitudes is crucial for a harmonious marriage. Discovering who is the spender and who is the saver, and how finances will be managed, are important things to know. It is also crucial to be on the same page and share the same goals. Finances can cause tension and allow for many misunderstandings, which can be eliminated or more easily worked out with greater understanding of one another’s views and opinions of money.

The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance. – Proverbs 21:5

Finding family-of-origin influences by examining how childhood experiences shape adult relationships through exploring and understanding inherited patterns.It is common to get comfortable with the way we do things.

For example, a woman thought that to cook a ham, you must cut off the ends. When questioned by her husband about this practice, she responded, “It is how my mother taught me to cook a ham.” Not really understanding why, she asked her mom, who explained that the ends were cut off because she didn’t have a pan large enough to fit the entire ham. This is an example of how we learn things from our family of origin and continue doing what we know.

Creating realistic expectations for marriage by encouraging healthy discussions about future goals and dreams and addressing myths about marriage. It is important for couples to head in the same direction regarding their marriage because unrealistic or uncommunicated expectations become a source of conflict and disappointment.

Couples will learn to see the big picture and to consider the needs of their future spouse, taking their eyes off themselves, in an attempt to understand and compromise. Expectations are good, but high expectations can be unhealthy, putting a strain on the relationship.

Exploring spiritual compatibility by encouraging conversations about faith, church involvement, prayer, and discipleship. Helping couples establish a shared vision for a Christ-centered home where it is a marriage of three – husband, wife, and Christ at the center.

Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken.– Ecclesiastes 4:12

Counselor’s Role

The counselor’s role in the SYMBIS process is to interpret the assessment results, help couples apply God’s truth to relationship challenges, and encourage spiritual growth alongside relational growth. The counselor also creates a safe place for honest conversations that address difficult issues by encouraging vulnerability and transparency and helps couples develop healthy problem-solving skills.

Speaking the truth in love.– Ephesians 4:15

By participating in premarital counseling, couples will benefit from

  • greater confidence (entering marriage with clarity and understanding
  • feeling prepared for future challenges)
  • stronger communication by learning practical skills to resolve conflict and developing healthy communication skills
  • developing a deeper emotional connection by gaining better understanding of one another
  • building trust and intimacy
  • gaining a stronger spiritual foundation where Christ is the center of the relationship
  • developing shared spiritual goals

Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain.– Psalm 127:1

Conclusion

Marriage is one of God’s greatest gifts and one of the most important commitments. Christ-centered premarital counseling provides couples with tools, wisdom, and biblical guidance before marriage begins. The SYMBIS Assessment offers valuable insights that help build a strong and lasting relationship. Invest today.

Are you engaged or seriously considering marriage? Discover how the SYMBIS Assessment and premarital counseling can help you build a strong marriage. Schedule your session today and begin building your covenant foundation.

Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. – 1 Peter 4:8

item.title: ADHD and Emotional Regulation: Why Feelings Hit Harder and What Can Help
item.description:
Emotional regulation is not a matter of just choosing to calm down. For people with ADHD, emotional regulation is the hardest part of the day. The distraction and impulsivity affect how emotions are felt, processed, and expressed.

Feelings hit hard and take longer to settle in this pattern of constraint, relationships, and derailed focus. ADHD and emotional regulation are tough when the brain works differently.

What ADHD and Emotional Regulation Actually Look Like

ADHD is often described as a focus problem. Focus is part of it, but the ability to regulate emotions also plays a big role. A significant number of people with ADHD find it difficult to manage the intensity and duration of their emotional responses.

Emotional regulation includes rapid mood shifts, low frustration tolerance, and a heightened sensitivity to rejection. These reflect real neurological differences in how the ADHD brain processes information.

Part of the brain that handles impulse control and emotional braking works differently in those with ADHD. The signal to slow down often arrives late or not at all. It’s just the biology of an ADHD brain.

Understanding this distinction is important because those with ADHD believe they are too emotional, reactive, or too much. Narratives like this do more damage than expected. The reality of the situation is that the brain is doing something specific and identifiable, which means it should be addressed as such.

Research suggests that there is an increase in the number of adults with ADHD who experience a degree of emotional dysregulation. This indicates that the experience is increasingly common. When individuals understand that what they experience has a neurological basis, it shifts the way they relate to themselves. This is one step toward real change.

Why Rejection Feels So Devastating

One of the most talked-about emotional experiences in the ADHD community is known as rejection-sensitive dysphoria. This is an intense emotional response that occurs with criticism, rejection, or failure.

Individuals without ADHD rarely take a critical comment to heart. However, an individual navigating ADHD with emotional regulation handles it differently. Challenges may be met with shame, anger, and withdrawal. What is labeled as drama is simply the nervous system registering something more intense than what most people experience.

Emotional sensitivity of this intensity can make everyday interactions seem exhausting. Social situations may carry extra weight when there’s a low level of awareness of something being said or done that may land the wrong way. When this happens, the fallout feels enormous, and some individuals with ADHD will begin to avoid similar situations where rejection is possible. This results in missed opportunities and isolation.

A pattern of avoidance can quietly reshape a person’s world. Friendships may thin out, and professional opportunities are left unpursued. The individual may not even realize there’s a connection between avoidance and sensitivity.

This is a cycle that requires recognition in order to understand the devastation of rejection. Recognizing this cycle requires an outside perspective from someone who can name the pattern and help the individual see it clearly. Finding this type of clarity is hard, and for many, it may become a turning point that moves them toward seeking help.

Scripture addresses this deep, emotional pain honestly. The book of Psalms contains many instances of raw and unfiltered cries from people who were overwhelmed and not pretending. (Psalm 22, 34, 55). God does not see this type of honesty as weakness. It is a model for processing what is real rather than burying it.

ADHD and Emotional Regulation Strategies That Help

Emotional dysregulation and ADHD respond to intervention. Different approaches have shown real promise, and most people find a combination that will work better than any single strategy.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy helps people identify thought patterns that may intensify emotional responses. After these patterns are identified, individuals can build accurate interpretations of triggering events. It is a process that takes time, but it does produce lasting change.

Mindfulness-based practices such as breathing exercises may create small but meaningful pauses between a trigger and a reaction. The pause creates a different outlook for those whose emotional brake pedal is slow. Core ADHD symptoms may be addressed through medication that reduces emotional intensity.

Structured daily routines are important to a regulated nervous system. When the body is depleted, a small lifestyle adjustment can make a big difference in emotional stability.

In Scripture, Paul addresses what it means to be content in all circumstances. He didn’t do this because it came naturally. He discussed it because it was something practiced and developed over time. This resonates deeply with people working on emotional regulation. It reduces the expectation of perfection and builds a skill, one day and one situation at a time, with patience for the process. (Philippians 4:11).

When patience extends to the tools, the right combination of strategies can be developed over time. There are no two people with ADHD who are exactly alike. This means that strategies will look different for each one. This is what makes the process worth pursuing. By approaching this process with honesty and support, the result is a meaningful and lasting change.

How Christian Counselors Can Support ADHD and Emotional Regulation

There is an added layer of shame that comes with the emotional intensity for Christians who struggle with ADHD. These individuals feel they should be more patient and more self-controlled. Christian counselors are trying to address the clinical and spiritual dimensions of this experience.

They help individuals separate biology and spirituality. What is a neurological reality versus a moral failure? This is valuable because these two things are not the same. The distinction can create freedom for someone who has spent years feeling like a spiritual failure because of how their brain works.

Christian counselors understand neurodevelopmental differences, which helps develop practical coping skills and hold space for grief, frustration, or other spiritual questions. Many adults are not diagnosed until their thirties or beyond. Discovering this brings up questions about what they experienced over the years, such as grief and anger. Being able to work through these discoveries with a counselor who integrates faith means the conversation doesn’t remain surface-level.

The integration of faith and practical coping skills matters more than one may think. They should not be separate from mental health. Many people use the lens of faith to understand various situations in life. A Christian counselor who understands this lens may offer clients a way to make sense of their diagnosis that will deepen their faith rather than challenge it.

Finding Steadiness When Emotions Run High

Moving forward with emotional regulation and ADHD doesn’t mean the individual is at the mercy of every feeling that arrives. There is a steadiness that comes from understanding what’s actually happening in the brain. When the individual stops suppressing or pretending that emotions are fine, they build skills that work with the ADHD nervous system. This is the awareness that changes things.

This process can also involve faith, which will create a foundation of knowing they are not defined by their worst emotional moments. Faith communities help them understand they are not alone in navigating these situations.

A Christian counselor who understands the spiritual and clinical aspects offers a framework of tools and perspective that will hold both without forcing a choice between them. This type of support is essential to making a difference for those who struggle with ADHD and emotional regulation.

If emotional dysregulation is affecting your daily life, your relationships, or someone you care about, you don’t have to figure it all out on your own. Reaching out for support isn’t a sign of weakness – it can be an important first step toward better understanding yourself and developing healthier ways to respond to difficult emotions.

In my work as a therapist, I help individuals better understand the connection between ADHD, emotions, relationships, and the patterns that can leave them feeling overwhelmed or stuck. If any of this sounds familiar and you feel counseling might be helpful, please consider reaching out to me – Joseph Bennett, LPC – to talk about what you’re experiencing and what your next steps might look like.

item.title: Journeying Through Loss: Understanding the Grief Process
item.description:
Despite our sometimes-stark differences, some things are common to us all. One of those things that we have in common with each other is that we grieve losses of various kinds. Grief is indeed one of the more universal human experiences, but it is also true that it remains poorly misunderstood and inadequately supported. Understanding the grief process can help you as you try to make sense of life after loss.

The Need to Pause After Loss

What is grief, and why do we need to grieve when we’ve experienced loss? Grief is the process we go through to come to terms with the fact that we’ve experienced a loss of some kind. Grief is how we adjust to no longer having a partner, whether because they’ve died or because you’ve undergone a divorce. Grief is the way you process having lost your community or sense of safety because you’ve moved or because of being a victim of crime.

When we experience loss, it comes with a swathe of emotions and the need to adjust to a new reality. You may experience feelings like shock and disbelief. Some experience deep anger, at themselves, at the person who left them, or at the Lord. Others feel a paralyzing fear as they contemplate what life will look like in the coming days, and others are numb. The question that faces a person who has experienced loss is usually, “What now?”

The many questions, doubts, emotions, and challenges that loss stirs up aren’t easy to come to terms with. For one thing, they imply that things are changing, and that what once could be counted on – the things that once made up your life as you knew it – are no longer the same. Now, you’ll have to adjust and figure out how to live without that loved one, without that same sense of place, or without the resources that you once could count on.

Our culture prizes forward movement, looking to the future, being productive, and possessing emotional composure. That often means that grief is treated as though it’s a temporary state that the individual should simply move through and get over as quickly as possible. Instead of seeing it as a deep wound that requires sustained, wise, and patient care, grief and loss are often treated like a superficial wound that you quickly dress and then forget about.

One of the tragedies of how our culture deals with loss and grief is that many people are left to grieve alone and in silence. If their grief shows, it sometimes invites reprimand, leading to an added sense of shame about the depth and duration of their grief and pain. In this way, grief is sometimes shuttered away and not given the chance to be dealt with properly. That grief doesn’t go away; it’s there, beneath the surface, and it affects your well-being in the long run.

There is a need to pause after loss, to give yourself time to grieve, to process things, and to begin rebuilding again. Grieving well doesn’t mean everything has to come to a standstill; life doesn’t afford us that luxury, as houses need to be cleaned, children need to be clothed, work needs doing, and bills need paying. Grieving does mean giving yourself space to work through the loss in the midst of everything else that may be happening.

How Grief Affects You

While grief is itself a process, going through that process has an impact on you. Facing your anger, sadness, sense of relief, or confusion about your loss isn’t easy. Often, people would rather avoid dealing with these complex and heavy emotions, and so it’s easier to bury these feelings, deny they exist, or simply find ways to not engage with them.

Grief affects you physically, emotionally, spiritually, and mentally. When you’ve experienced significant loss, it affects you spiritually, as you ask questions such as “Why did this happen?” “Where is God in the midst of all this?” or “What does this mean?” Loss and the grief that follows can leave you asking these deep, existential questions about meaning, purpose, and God’s presence in the darkest valleys.

Physically, your grief can manifest as disruptions in your sleeping patterns. Some people struggle to fall and stay asleep, while others find themselves sleeping far more than usual. You may also find that your appetite changes, you feel tired quite often, your immune system feels like it’s weakened and under constant attack, and you carry a sort of heaviness that weighs on you in ways you struggle to describe.

Grief also affects you cognitively in various ways. Some people find it harder to remember things; it feels like your mind is losing grasp of things like names, places, faces, and other details. Grief also affects your ability to concentrate, and it can also make it harder to make decisions, even about simple everyday matters like what to wear and in what order to perform daily chores.

In terms of your emotions, grief surfaces a variety of feelings including sadness, guilt, anxiety, longing, confusion, relief, and anger. These emotions point to the fact that you’ve lost something or someone that mattered to you, and when that bond is severed, it produces a variety of emotional responses. Even complicated relationships, like with an estranged parent, can manifest in these emotions.

Grief will often run its natural course. That’s not to say that grief is a linear process, or that it comes to an end. Rather, it’s to say that you learn to live with the loss, to carry on. However, grief can also become complicated, whether by being intensified, prolonged, or leaving you feeling stuck in such a way that you’re not carrying on with the business of living.

This complicated grief is marked by an intense and persistent yearning for what you’ve lost, having difficulty accepting the loss, feeling bitter or emotionally numb, and being unable to engage with life again. This kind of complicated grief happens when a person experiences sudden or traumatic loss. It also occurs when a person doesn’t have adequate social support to help them grieve, or when they are ambivalent toward the loss.

Looking Beyond the Five Stages of Grief

Grief is, at its heart, how we come to terms with loss. One of the more common ways to understand grief is through the Kübler-Ross model of grief, which has five stages. These stages are denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. What this model has done is help people understand that grief is a process, and not a single event. This is helpful, especially in those circumstances where people are too quick to move on from loss.

Having said that, the Kübler-Ross model of grief is also often misunderstood by people. Some people assume that the five stages name a neat progression from one emotional state to the next, and then out the other side with acceptance. Grief isn’t a linear journey that takes you from denial to acceptance in an orderly fashion. These stages don’t occur in order; they also don’t occur once, and they don’t apply to everyone or every kind of loss in the same way.

Grief often occurs as waves, and you could find yourself feeling anger and depression on the same day. Sometimes a particular experience surfaces a specific feeling, like when you walk in a familiar park and find it hard to accept that your loved one is just gone.

Another way to understand grief is through what’s known as the dual process model of grief, which describes how people experiencing loss will go between loss-orientation, which is when they’re engaging directly with the memories, the grief, and the pain of loss, and restoration-orientation, which is them attending to new roles they take up, life changes that the loss necessitated, and looking to the future.

Dealing with loss in a healthy way means moving between both orientations. Life won’t look like a steady progression through the various stages of grief; rather, it’ll be more of a non-linear, dynamic process that doesn’t look the same for any two people dealing with loss.

As you journey through grief, you don’t have to do it alone. Whether the grief and loss that you’re dealing with is old or more recent, whether it’s clean-cut or complicated, and whether you’ve even named that grief for yourself, you can have respectful company along with you on the journey. Christian counseling offers you a structured and safe place to be honest about what you’ve lost, how you feel about it, and what you need to help you go on.

If you want to unpack your grief and loss, you can browse our online counselor directory or reach out to our office today to schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor. Your counselor will journey with you, without placing you under the pressure of a timeline or a cultural script that you should follow in dealing with your grief.

item.title: Finding the Right Help: The Value of Naming Addictions Like Chemical Dependency
item.description:
When someone starts looking for mental health support, they expect clear answers. Instead, most likely, you’ll hear a mix of terms that leave you wondering what applies to you, especially when it comes to addiction therapy.

You reach out for help because something doesn’t feel right. You’re tired, anxious, and using substances to get through the day. Yet most people say they don’t really know which category they fall into.

Is it addiction? Is it chemical dependency? Substance abuse? Use Abuse? Drug Abuse? Or something else entirely? The truth is, the words used to describe your struggle can shape the kind of help you receive, and whether that help truly fits your needs.

It’s easy to assume they all mean the same thing, but those terms point to different realities. When the wrong one is used, the treatment plan can miss the real issue. You might end up addressing symptoms instead of causes, or focusing on behavior when the body itself is dependent.

Understanding which one describes what you’re facing is the first step toward getting help that works for you.

Why Language Decides the Direction of Your Recovery

Language in mental health and recovery isn’t just technical; it’s also directional. The words professionals use determine what kind of support you’ll be offered, what insurance covers, and how your progress is measured.

If someone treats chemical dependency as general addiction, they may overlook the body’s physical need for the substance. If they treat substance abuse as chemical dependency, they may over‑medicalize what’s primarily behavioral.

When the terminology doesn’t match the reality, recovery becomes harder. You might feel like you’re doing everything right but still not improving, because the treatment isn’t addressing the right layer of the problem.

How These Terms Came to Be

The confusion around addiction language didn’t happen overnight. The words used to describe addiction didn’t appear all at once. They grew out of different moments in history, each shaped by how society viewed substance use at the time.

Moreover, these shifts weren’t just linguistic; they changed how people were treated and perceived.

Alcoholism became common in the 1930s and 1940s. In the early 1900s, people struggling with alcohol were often seen as weak or immoral. When Alcoholics Anonymous began in the 1930s, the term alcoholism reframed drinking as a disease rather than a failure of character.

Drug abuse entered the public vocabulary in the 1960s and 1970s when public concern shifted toward drugs. Governments and health agencies started using the phrase drug abuse, which focused more on control and legality than healing. The word abuse carried judgment, and many people were treated as criminals rather than patients.

Chemical dependency appeared in the 1970s and 1980s, when treatment centers introduced the concept of chemical dependency to highlight the body’s physical reliance on an actual substance. This helped professionals separate biological dependence from emotional or behavioral addiction. It also made space for medical detox programs and more structured rehabilitation.

Substance abuse became a clinical term as research expanded in the 1980s and 1990s. Substance became a broader clinical term, covering alcohol, prescription medication, and other substances.

Substance use disorder replaced older labels in the DSM‑5. This newer language recognizes that addiction exists on a spectrum, from mild misuse to severe dependency, and aims to reduce the shame of the word ‘abuse’ while improving accuracy.

Each transition reflected a growing understanding of addiction as both biological and psychological. But it also created overlap, and sometimes confusion, between terms that sound interchangeable but aren’t.

Understanding the Differences

To make sense of these words, it helps to see how they relate to one another.

  • Addiction describes a pattern of compulsive use despite harm. It’s broad and behavioral
  • Chemical dependency focuses on the body’s physical reliance on a substance. It’s biological and measurable
  • Substance abuse refers to harmful or risky use, not necessarily dependence
  • Alcoholism is specific to alcohol and includes both physical and emotional dependence
  • Substance use disorder is the modern diagnostic term that covers all levels of severity

When you understand these distinctions, you start to see why treatment plans differ. Detox addresses chemical dependency. Counseling addresses addiction patterns. Support groups address emotional recovery. Each piece matters, but only if it matches the real issue.

The Emotional Side of Getting the Words Right

There’s also a personal reason to understand these terms. When you know what you’re facing, you stop blaming yourself for not “trying hard enough.” You begin to see that recovery isn’t a test of character, but a process of healing both body and mind.

Accurate language helps you talk to loved ones, counselors, and even yourself with more clarity. It turns vague frustration into specific understanding. Instead of saying, “I can’t stop,” you start saying, “My body has adapted to this substance, and I need help to reverse that.” That change of mindset changes everything.

If you’re unsure which term fits your situation, start by noticing what’s happening in your body and emotions.

Why Chemical Dependency Deserves Its Own Attention

Chemical dependency is unique because it involves the body’s chemistry adapting to a substance. The brain and nervous system begin to rely on it to function normally. When the substance is removed, the body reacts, sometimes severely.

That’s why treating chemical dependency requires medical oversight and gradual stabilization. It’s not just about willpower or mindset. It’s about helping the body relearn balance.

Ignoring this distinction can be serious. Without proper medical support, withdrawal can be dangerous. Without emotional support, relapse becomes more likely. Both sides need to be addressed, but in the right order.

How to Tell What Kind of Help You Need

Ask yourself:

  • Do I feel physically unwell when I stop using a certain substance?
  • Do I rely on it to feel normal or calm?
  • Do I use it to manage emotions rather than physical cravings?
  • Have I tried to quit but found my body reacting strongly?

If your body reacts to a specific chemical component, then that points toward chemical dependency. If the struggle feels more emotional or behavioral, it may be addiction. Either way, clarity helps professionals guide you toward the right combination of medical and therapeutic support.

Once you have a clearer sense of what’s happening, you then need steps to make sure you’re getting appropriate care.

Getting the Right Help

Ask for definitions: When a counselor or doctor uses a term, ask what it means and how it applies to you.

Describe your symptoms clearly: Include both physical and emotional experiences.

Seek integrated care: Look for professionals who address both body and mind; medical detox paired with counseling or faith‑based support.

Avoid self‑diagnosis: Online definitions can help you learn, but professional evaluation ensures accuracy.

Keep language consistent: When talking to different providers, use the same term so your care stays aligned.

These steps may sound simple, but they prevent confusion that can delay recovery. They also help you feel more in control of your healing process.

Faith communities sometimes use different words, such as bondage, brokenness, or deliverance, to describe addiction. Those words carry emotional truth, but they don’t replace medical understanding.

Bringing both perspectives together creates a fuller picture. Faith offers hope and meaning; clinical language offers precision and safety. When both are respected, recovery becomes more holistic and sustainable.

Getting the right help starts with being understood. When professionals use the right term, treatment becomes targeted. When you understand those terms yourself, you become an active participant in your healing.

Chemical dependency isn’t just another word for addiction; it’s a specific condition that requires specific care. Knowing that difference can protect your health, your relationships, and your sense of hope.

If you’re unsure which term fits what you’re facing, reach out to a professional therapist who is trained to help you sort through it. The right words lead to the right kind of help, and that help can change your life.

Consider connecting with a counselor listed on this site or calling the numbers on the screen to start that conversation today.

item.title: Can a Marriage Survive Infidelity? 10 Christian Principles for Healing and Recovery
item.description:
Discovering that your spouse has been unfaithful can feel like the ground has disappeared underneath you. The person you trusted and built a life with has betrayed that trust. Suddenly, you may find yourself questioning your marriage, your memories, your judgment, and your future. And then comes the big question: “Can our marriage actually survive this?”

The short answer is: “yes.” Marriages can survive infidelity. Some couples even go on to build marriages that are more honest, connected, and intentional than they were before. But that doesn’t mean every marriage should survive infidelity. You do have a choice in whether or not you stay in the marriage. And from a Christian perspective, distinction is incredibly important.

What counts as infidelity?

When we hear the words “affair” or “infidelity,” we often think of a sexual relationship outside of marriage. But this can take different forms.

An emotional affair may involve developing a secret emotional intimacy or romantic attachment to someone outside the marriage. Sexual infidelity that doesn’t become physical can include sexting, explicit photos, sexual conversations, or online sexual relationships. Physical infidelity can range from kissing or sexual touching to intercourse. And some affairs become full romantic relationships involving emotional and physical intimacy over time.

Rather than defining infidelity by one particular act, it can be helpful to look at the boundaries of marriage, secrecy, and betrayal of trust. Ask yourself if a romantic, emotional, or sexual relationship developed outside the boundaries you and your spouse had for your marriage. Was it kept secret because you knew your spouse would feel hurt or betrayed if they knew?

Someone might say, “But we never had sex.” That may be true. But infidelity does not have to involve sex. Emotional or romantic relationships can also cross the boundaries of a marriage and create a deep sense of betrayal.

First: Staying is a choice

As a Christian, you may feel pressure to save your marriage no matter what. After infidelity, you might even wonder, “If I leave, does that mean I didn’t forgive enough? Did I not pray enough? Am I giving up instead of trusting God?”

But the Bible does not tell a betrayed spouse that they must stay in a marriage after sexual immorality. In Matthew 19:9, Jesus says that divorce is permitted in cases of sexual immorality. In other words, Scripture gives the betrayed spouse permission to leave. But permission to leave is not a command to leave.

You may decide that too much trust has been broken and you cannot rebuild the marriage. Or you may decide that you want to stay and work toward reconciliation. This is a deep personal decision that deserves time, prayer, wisdom, and support.

Choosing to stay does not make you weak. And choosing to leave after infidelity does not automatically mean you have failed God. If you choose to stay, though, healing will require more than simply deciding not to get divorced. The relationship itself will need to heal.

Drawing from my work with couples and betrayal trauma, along with principles from Gottman Method Couples Therapy, here are ten important, faith-based principles for recovery.

Come clean

One of the most damaging patterns after infidelity is what we in the field often refer to as “trickle truth.”

The betrayed spouse discovers something; the unfaithful partner may completely deny it or only admit to part of it, until more information comes out later. The person who had the affair may say they were withholding information to “protect” their spouse. But withholding the truth also allows them to control the narrative.

We know that every new disclosure can create another betrayal. This erodes any of the fragile trust that may have been built back since discovery. The hurt spouse may ask themselves: “What else don’t I know? Can I trust anything you’ve told me?” Healing cannot truly begin while significant information is still being withheld. Your spouse needs an intentional disclosure process rather than numerous discovery days.

That doesn’t mean sharing unnecessarily graphic, intimate details that could worsen intrusive images. But the key facts of the infidelity need to come into the light as soon as possible. The simple fact is you cannot rebuild trust on top of secrecy.

Atone and take responsibility

The Gottman approach to healing after an affair describes three phases: atone, attune, and attach. Healing begins with atonement, or taking responsibility for what happened.

If you were the unfaithful partner, this is not the time to say, “I was lonely,” “You weren’t affectionate,” or “We were already having problems.” Those struggles in the marriage may be real, and there will be a time to talk about them. But they do not make your spouse responsible for your decision to cross the boundaries of the marriage.

Atonement means being able to say, “I did this. I hurt you. I am responsible for my choices.” It means showing genuine remorse, answering reasonable questions honestly, and allowing your spouse to be hurt without immediately defending yourself or shifting the blame.

The Bible also connects healing with bringing sin into the open rather than hiding it. Proverbs 28:13 teaches that the person who hides or covers their sin will not prosper, but the person who confesses it and turns away from it finds mercy.

And repentance is more than simply saying, “I’m sorry.” In 2 Corinthians 7:10–11, Paul describes godly sorrow as the kind of sorrow that leads to repentance and produces real change. That distinction matters after infidelity. Your spouse does not only need to hear that you are sorry. Over time, they need to see honesty, responsibility, openness, and changed behavior. They need to slowly begin recognizing that this marriage is becoming safe again.

Understand the trauma and unite against it.

Many people do not understand that betrayal can be traumatic. After discovering infidelity, the hurt partner may feel constantly on guard. They may experience intrusive thoughts or images, nightmares, anxiety, difficulty trusting, or a strong need to know that they are safe.

Triggers can also show up unexpectedly. A phone notification, a certain place, a song, a date, a photo, a sexual experience, or even a random comment can suddenly bring the pain rushing back. The hurt partner may wonder, “Why can’t I just move forward?”

The truth is that some people experience symptoms like post-traumatic stress after betrayal. Their mind and body may continue reacting to reminders of what happened, even when they desperately want to move forward. Understanding this can change the way a couple responds to those difficult moments.

Instead of: “Why are you bringing this up again?”

Try: “This brought the hurt back up again. How can we get through this moment together?”

Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says that “two are better than one” and describes how one person can help the other when they fall. That can be a beautiful picture of recovery. If you have both chosen to work toward rebuilding the marriage, you can begin learning how to face the pain together instead of turning against each other.

The goal is not for the hurt partner to simply “get over it.” The goal is for both of you to recognize when the betrayal is affecting the relationship and learn how to respond as a team. Instead of fighting each other, you can begin fighting together for the healing of your marriage.

Accept your choice to stay

If you choose to stay, know that staying may be incredibly hard. People around you may have opinions. Friends, family members, pastors, or mentors may tell you what they think you should do. You may even question your own decision at times.

If you have prayerfully chosen to see whether your marriage can heal, there will come a point when you need to radically accept the decision you are making for today. Radical acceptance does not mean saying, “What happened was okay.”

It does not mean excusing the betrayal, minimizing your pain, or promising that you will stay no matter what happens next. It simply means: “This happened. I wish it had not happened, but I cannot change the past. Today, I am choosing to see if healing and reconciliation are possible.”

You do not have to know exactly what your marriage will look like a year from now. You do not need 100% certainty that everything will work out. You can simply take the next faithful step in front of you.

If reconciliation is what you have prayerfully chosen to pursue, there can be something deeply God-honoring in extending grace, seeking healing, and working toward restoration after you have been deeply hurt. That does not make the betrayal acceptable. It means you are choosing to see whether something broken can be rebuilt.

Galatians 6:9 offers encouragement for seasons like this: “Let us not become weary in doing good.” This verse is a reminder that there is a harvest when we do not give up. Healing after betrayal can be slow and exhausting. Permit yourself to take it one day at a time.

Limit third-party influence

Support matters after betrayal, but not all support will help you heal. If you have chosen to work toward reconciliation, surround yourself with people who can support that decision and walk prayerfully beside you through the process.

If every conversation ends with someone saying, “I can’t believe you’re staying,” or constantly questioning your decision, their voice can eventually become louder than your own. That can make an already difficult season even harder.

You are allowed to be careful about who has access to this vulnerable part of your marriage. Proverbs 13:20 tells us, “Walk with the wise and become wise.” During a difficult season, the people walking beside you matter.

Look for a few trusted people who will pray with you, encourage you, listen without judgment, and speak truth when you need to hear it. You need people who understand that supporting you does not mean pretending the betrayal was okay. It means respecting your prayerful decision to pursue healing and being willing to walk beside you as you do.

This does not mean isolating yourself or avoiding healthy accountability. You still need people who will be honest with you and who care about the health and safety of your marriage. But you can choose people who are able to say, “I know this is hard. I’m here. I’ll pray with you. I’ll support you as you seek God’s wisdom and take this one step at a time.”

You do not need everyone to understand your decision. You need a few safe, wise, prayerful people who are willing to walk with you through it.

Be patient with healing

Healing rarely draws a straight line. You may have several good weeks and then suddenly have a really hard day. That does not mean you are back at the beginning, even though it can often feel that way. The betrayed spouse may love their partner and still feel angry. They may forgive and still grieve. They may have a wonderful weekend together and then experience a painful trigger on Monday.

The unfaithful partner needs to resist saying, “We’ve already talked about this,” or “When are you going to let this go?” And the betrayed partner needs to have patience with themselves. Psalm 147:3 reminds us that God “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” Healing takes time, and God can be present in the process.

Sometimes recovery feels like two steps forward and one step backward. But one step backward does not erase the two steps you already took.

Replace secrecy with transparency

If secrecy created the hurt, transparency can help rebuild safety. This may mean being more open about phones, communication, schedules, friendships, social media, or contact with certain people. The goal is not for one spouse to become a permanent detective. Transparency simply says: “I understand why you don’t trust me right now, and I am willing to live in a way that helps you feel safe trusting me again.”

Scripture values this kind of honesty. Proverbs 12:22 says that “the Lord delights in people who are trustworthy.” Trust is not something the betrayed spouse owes simply because an apology was given. Trust is rebuilt slowly through honesty, consistency, and repeated experiences of trustworthiness.

Learn to attune to each other again

Eventually, healing needs to become about more than the affair itself. This is where the Gottman concept of attunement becomes important. Can you listen without immediately defending yourself? Can you begin understanding what your spouse is feeling and experiencing? Can you have honest conversations about intimacy, loneliness, stress, sex, faith, resentment, and unmet needs?

James 1:19 encourages us to be “quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry.” That can be an important mindset as you learn how to hear and understand each other again. Your marriage may have had real problems before the affair, and those problems deserve attention.

But remember, relationship problems can be explored without making them responsible for the affair. The marriage belongs to both people. The decision to cross its boundaries belongs to the person who made that choice.

Rebuild trust in small moments

Trust usually does not return in one giant moment. It comes back through hundreds of small ones. After betrayal, it can be tempting to look for the big conversation, apology, or promise that will finally make everything feel okay again. But trust is usually rebuilt much more slowly.

  • You said you would call, and you called
  • You answered the uncomfortable question honestly
  • Your spouse became triggered, and instead of becoming defensive or frustrated, you stayed present
  • You followed through
  • You listened
  • You kept your word
  • And then you did it again tomorrow

Jesus says in Luke 16:10, “Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much.” While this passage is not specifically about marriage, the principle of faithfulness in the small things applies beautifully to rebuilding trust.

Faithfulness is not only found in big promises. It is demonstrated in the small, everyday choices to be honest, consistent, patient, and dependable. After infidelity, your spouse may not be ready to trust your words yet. Give them time to experience your actions. You do not rebuild trust by asking someone to trust you again. You rebuild it by becoming trustworthy again, one small choice at a time.

Build something new

After an affair, the goal is not to get your old marriage back. That marriage has been changed by what happened, and in many ways, it is something you will need to grieve. If you choose reconciliation, the question centers around what kind of marriage you want to build now.

Maybe it is a marriage with more honesty, healthier boundaries, deeper emotional intimacy, better communication, and a faith lived out in the difficult parts of marriage- not just on Sunday.

In Isaiah 43:18–19, God tells His people not to remain stuck in the past because He says, “I am doing a new thing.” This passage offers us a beautiful reminder that God can bring something new out of a painful season.

This is where the Gottman concept of “Attach” becomes meaningful. You begin intentionally reconnecting, creating new experiences together, and building a different marriage: one shaped by greater honesty, understanding, and faithfulness.

You are not pretending the betrayal never happened, and you are not trying to recreate what was there before. That marriage is gone. But if you both choose healing, with God’s help, you can begin building something new.

Choosing What Comes Next

If you are standing in the aftermath of infidelity, you may desperately want someone to tell you what to do, but you do not have to make every decision today. You are allowed to grieve, ask questions, establish boundaries, seek wise counsel, and take time.

From a Christian perspective, you may have biblical permission to leave. But you also have permission to stay. Choosing reconciliation does not mean pretending the betrayal wasn’t serious. Forgiveness does not remove accountability. Grace does not require the absence of boundaries.

If you choose to stay, the goal should not simply be keeping your marriage intact. The goal is healing. The healing will not happen quickly or easily. But with time, grace, truth, and intentional work, a couple can build a new marriage where trust can slowly grow again.

Help is out there

If you are trying to make sense of betrayal, rebuild trust, or determine what healing looks like for your marriage, you don’t have to navigate it alone. You can reach out to schedule a counseling appointment for support with infidelity recovery and betrayal trauma.

I have also created two faith-based healing guides available on Amazon:

When Covenant Was Broken is for the betrayed partner navigating the hurt, trauma, questions, and complicated emotions that follow infidelity.

When You Broke Covenant is for the partner who was unfaithful and wants to take responsibility, understand their spouse’s pain, and begin rebuilding trust.

Both combine practical healing tools with Christian faith and biblical encouragement. You don’t have to know exactly what the future of your marriage looks like today to start with the next faithful step in healing.

item.title: Can EMDR Help When Grief Has Left Me Feeling Empty?
item.description:
For many people, grief doesn’t feel like pain. It feels like nothing at all. A strange emptiness that can last for weeks or years, making it hard to connect with life or hope. You may not notice when your grief turns into emptiness. You just realize one day that nothing moves you anymore.

You may find yourself going through the motions, doing what needs to be done, but feeling disconnected from life. That kind of numbness can be confusing because it doesn’t fit the picture most people have of grief.

Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, or EMDR, is usually known for helping people recover from trauma. What many don’t know is that it can also help when grief leaves you feeling hollow inside. Many therapists have used it as a practical tool for helping your mind and body reconnect after loss in ways that feel natural and human again.

When Grief Turns into Emotional Numbness

After the loss of a loved one, your body and mind naturally try to protect you. Sometimes that protection means shutting down feelings that seem too painful to face. You may not even realize it’s happening and just notice that you feel numb inside.

  • You stop reacting to things that used to move you
  • You feel detached from people you care about
  • You lose interest in routines that once gave you comfort

This is your nervous system trying to keep you safe. Unfortunately, over time, that safety mechanism can lead to isolation. You start to feel like you’re watching your own life from a distance, unable to step back into it.

Why Emotional Disconnection Happens

Grief doesn’t only affect your thoughts; it changes how your body processes emotion. When pain feels unbearable, your brain may block certain memories or sensations to help you function. That’s why some people describe feeling frozen in time or dead inside.

Action-oriented therapies like eye movement desensitization and reprocessing can help by gently unlocking those frozen responses. Through guided, tiny, deliberate eye movements or other forms of bilateral stimulation, EMDR helps your brain reprocess memories and emotions that were stored in survival mode. The focus is on helping your body recognize that the danger has passed so it can begin to feel again.

What EMDR Does Differently

Traditional talk therapy helps you understand grief through conversation. EMDR works on a deeper level: the part of your brain that holds emotional memory. When you experience loss, your mind stores not just the event but the sensations, thoughts, and physical reactions that came with it.

EMDR helps those memories move from a raw, reactive state into a more integrated one. You may start to notice that memories of your loved one feel less painful and more peaceful. You could also find that eventually the emptiness begins to soften, replaced by small instances of connection: a song that suddenly feels meaningful again, or a memory that brings warmth instead of ache.

When You Feel Empty but Still Function

One of the hardest parts of grief-related numbness is that you can still appear fine. You go to work, take care of responsibilities, and even laugh at times. But inside, there’s a quiet sense of absence.

EMDR helps bridge that gap between functioning and feeling. It gives your nervous system permission to reconnect with emotion safely. You don’t have to force tears or talk endlessly about the loss. The process works gradually, helping your body release tension and your mind rediscover emotional rhythm.

How EMDR Supports Healing Beyond Tears

Healing doesn’t always mean crying or expressing sadness. Sometimes it means learning to feel again in rather ordinary ways. EMDR helps you notice sensations you may have tuned out, like the warmth of sunlight, the comfort of a familiar smell, and the sound of laughter.

These reconnections with ordinary things matter because they remind your body that life still holds meaning.

How Healing Through EMDR Happens

Healing through EMDR may not happen instantly; usually, it works slowly, subtly, and in a deeply personal way. Bit by bit, you’ll start to notice changes like:

  • Feeling more emotionally responsive to everyday life
  • Remembering your loved one with less pain and more peace
  • Experiencing fewer physical symptoms of tension or fatigue
  • Reconnecting with faith, creativity, or relationships that once felt distant

Each session helps your brain reprocess stored emotions so they no longer feel overwhelming or unreachable. Over time, you begin to experience grief as part of your story, rather than as something that defines or drains you.

In time, you begin to find that grief becomes less about emptiness and more about remembrance, the kind that honors what was lost. While EMDR helps on a neurological level, emotional reconnection also grows through deliberate, intentional habits.

Simple Ways to Support Emotional Reconnection Alongside EMDR

Write without censoring: Let your thoughts spill onto paper, not to analyze them, but to give them space.

Practice calm movement: Regular walking, stretching, or breathing exercises help release stored tension.

Learn to enjoy shared silence: Connect with others through shared silence. Sometimes a person’s presence matters more than words.

Allow yourself small joys: You don’t have to feel guilty for moments of laughter or calm. There are signs that your nervous system is healing. None of this can truly replace therapy, but simple, intentional steps like this complement it.

They help you rebuild emotional rhythm in daily life while EMDR works on deeper layers of healing.

Why Feeling Empty Deserves Compassion, Not Judgment

Many people assume grief should look a certain way, with tears, sadness, and visible emotion all the time. Yet, emotional emptiness and the complete lack of those emotions is just as painful. It’s a sign that your body has been through something profound and is in defense mode.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing can help you meet that emptiness with compassion instead of frustration. It teaches your mind that feeling disconnected isn’t failure; it’s part of how healing unfolds. When you stop fighting the numbness and start understanding it, space opens for emotion to return naturally.

Relearning How to Feel Safe in Your Own Body

One of the quiet gifts of approaches like EMDR is helping you feel safe again, not just mentally, but physically. Grief can make your body feel foreign, as if you’re living inside someone else’s skin. Through EMDR, you begin to trust your body’s signals again. You notice when you’re tense, when you’re calm, and when you’re ready to feel.

That sense of safety is what allows emotion to return. You don’t have to chase it; it comes back when your body knows it’s ready.

When to Reach Out for More Help

If grief has left you feeling empty for months or years, EMDR therapy is one option among many, but it works gently and effectively for people who feel disconnected after loss. A trained therapist can help you explore whether EMDR fits your needs and guide you through the process at a pace that feels right.

Feeling empty after grief doesn’t mean you’ve stopped caring or forgotten. It means your body and mind are still protecting you from pain that felt too deep to face. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing offers a way to reconnect: not by forcing emotion, but by helping your nervous system remember how to feel safely again.

If you’ve been living in that quiet space where everything feels muted, don’t hesitate to ask for a professional to help. The team listed on this site can help you explore EMDR and other approaches that support emotional healing in a way that works for you.

You can also call the numbers on the screen to speak with someone who understands what you’re going through. Healing begins when you stop trying to feel normal and start allowing yourself to feel human again.

item.title: The Effectiveness and Challenges of DBT for Teens
item.description:
If you have a teen who is struggling in any area of life, you might have considered involving them in DBT, or at least wondered if DBT is right for them. Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) is an intensive form of talk therapy originally developed to help people with borderline personality disorder.

Now DBT helps people develop skills for managing crises, dealing with strong emotions, and improving communication in relationships. For these reasons, DBT for teens has become increasingly popular in recent years.

DBT is not suitable or effective for everyone. It is comprehensive, highly structured, and can feel demanding for some teens, especially those who are under academic pressure. DBT typically requires at least six months of involvement to see the best results, which is a commitment many teens and their families are not willing or even able to commit to. Still, it can be adapted to suit your needs and is worth considering as a potentially effective form of therapy for a struggling adolescent.

The Building Blocks of DBT

The goal of DBT is to reduce life-threatening behaviors like suicide attempts, self-harm, eating disorders, substance use, or severe emotional dysregulation. It helps by giving you the tools to cope and develop a balanced mindset with regulated emotions. This might sound like a tall order or even an impossible goal, but DBT is developed to help you over a long period of time.

DBT helps you develop skills using mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotional regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness. Firstly, with mindfulness, you are encouraged to be curious about your emotions, thoughts, and responses to the stressors in your life. The key is not to be judgmental of yourselves or others, but to pay gentle attention to your experiences. When you take notice of the things you are thinking and feeling, you have begun to regain control over the chaos in your life.

The next building block of DBT for teens is stress tolerance. There are many crises to navigate as an adolescent, and sometimes it feels as if you are inundated. DBT teaches you how to raise yourself to the surface of the stress, and, over time, to effortlessly navigate difficult situations.

Next, you will learn how to regulate your emotions. This is a vital skill that takes a long time to develop. However, learning how to calm your emotions when they have become overwhelming is a skill that you will carry far into life. Emotional regulation is a vital skill to have and one that you can hone and strengthen over time.

Lastly, DBT will teach you interpersonal effectiveness. This is a blanket term for a host of useful skills, like communicating your needs confidently, setting boundaries, and maintaining self-respect in any relationship. These are things that even adults take decades to learn. DBT could give you a head start as an adolescent in developing skills that you will use for the rest of your life.

The Structure of DBT for Teens

While every therapist is unique, there is a general format for DBT that most therapists will try to follow. Generally, you will attend weekly individual sessions with your therapist where you check in, set goals for your time together, learn or practice skills, and go over homework for the week ahead.

A typical individual session with your therapist will last anywhere between 45 minutes and an hour, after which time you might feel exhausted. Your therapist will also schedule sessions that involve family members, who will also develop skills and receive homework for the coming week.

DBT also typically involves a group therapy session with other teens. These are sort of like a class where you learn and practice new skills together. You might have to do some role-playing exercises and practice communication skills with partners.

A common communication exercise in DBT is DEAR MAN, which stands for Describe, Express, Assert, Reinforce, Mindful, Appear confident, and Negotiate. Another exercise frequently used in DBT for teens is Walking the Middle Path, which helps develop flexible thinking and better problem-solving skills.

Besides the weekly individual session with your therapist and group session, you will also complete homework, which typically involves filling out diary cards and worksheets focusing on your emotions and current experiences. Additionally, your therapist will call you once a week to do a brief coaching session. You might talk about something you are currently facing or a hypothetical situation. The phone session is an opportunity to rehearse a skill you have learned that will apply to the situation.

DBT is not a form of therapy you can approach nonchalantly; it is structured and highly comprehensive. Overall, it takes no less than six months for you to fully incorporate the skills you learn in DBT into your life. You will learn the balance of accepting your emotions in a non-judgmental way, while also changing the way you think and behave in certain situations so that you can cope with stress in healthier ways.

The Challenges of DBT for Teens

While the statistics show just how successful DBT is for teens, it is not a case of one-size-fits-all. Statistics also show high dropout rates and disengagement for teens and their families. Some people never realize how involved this form of therapy is, or else they fail to maintain the momentum required for long-term results.

Sometimes life changes so rapidly that your involvement in the process is hampered. Weeks turn to months, and eventually it’s too hard to pick up from wherever you left off with your therapist. Some people face logistical barriers, too. Intensive therapy is hard for adults, let alone teenagers who have exams, academic pressures, and frequent relationship crises. The things that impact your mental health and necessitate therapy are also the things that steal focus and inhibit your progress.

While some people thrive with the rigid structure and demands of DBT, others find the formal structure clinical and repetitive. People with intellectual disabilities or neurodiverse disorders will likely not gain much from DBT, and it may cause more harm than good in the long run. DBT does not match with some cultures. Certain families will decide that DBT is not a good fit for them at all.

DBT for teens requires regular involvement from parents or primary caregivers and sometimes siblings. They are also required to learn communication and emotional regulation skills, so that the family grows and matures as a unit. However, this can be demanding for certain families who have limited time and demanding schedules. They might have their own unresolved emotional issues, which they are not ready to face. While these factors are legitimate, they also hamper progress.

DBT is as structured, demanding, and intense as it is effective. There are certain issues both teens and adults face that can only be helped by therapies like DBT. Sometimes it is helpful simply knowing that you have options, and that there is a form of therapy specifically designed to impact the specific struggle you are facing. DBT for teens provides an opportunity for a family to learn, heal, and grow together. If you are willing to do the work today, you will reap a harvest tomorrow.

Learn More About DBT for Teens

If you are curious about DBT, if you would like to discuss it with a professional, or if you would like to see if it is available in your area, please get in touch with us. You may speak with our online reception team, who will help connect you to a counselor for more information. We also host an online catalog of counselors whom you can reach out to directly if you would prefer. We hope that we can help you find the form of therapy and counseling that best suits you.

item.title: Emotional Abuse and the Invisible Wounds That Run Deep
item.description:
There are times when a person will walk away from a relationship with no visible bruises or physical evidence of harm. Society sees this and says it wasn’t that bad. But there is abuse that doesn’t require physical force to cause real damage. Emotional abuse works gradually through words, silence, manipulation, and control to reshape the way a person sees themselves, the relationship, and their sense of what is normal.

For survivors, the hardest part of this experience is convincing themselves that what happened was real. There may be no photographs of the damage and no visible injuries to point to that clearly mark a line that was crossed. There’s no way to define a single incident that moved into the realm of unacceptable behavior. But something inside of these individuals knows that this abuse was real.

There’s a confusion that comes with this invisible injury, and it is part of the harm. Pain that isn’t seen becomes easy to minimize for others who weren’t there, and for the person who carried it quietly for years.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

What Emotional Abuse Actually Looks Like

Emotional abuse does not arrive with a loud voice or an obvious presence. It doesn’t always show up in screaming, in a match, or in clear-cut cruelty. It accumulates slowly in small moments that seem almost manageable.

It could show up as a partner who frames constant criticism as concern or maybe a parent who uses guilt as a primary tool to shape behavior. It may be the friend who dismisses your feelings so consistently that you stop sharing them altogether. These are the patterns that, over time, will produce something in an individual that is deeper than hurt feelings.

Individuals who experience emotional abuse often begin to question their own perception, yet they are right to trust what they sense. Christian counselors are trained to work with individuals who cannot identify what is wrong but do recognize that something is off – feeling depleted, anxious, and small.

Without the presence of a dramatic defining incident, emotional abuse can be harder to name and harder to leave. When there’s no clear moment to point to, doubt fills the space where certainty should be.

For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. – Ephesians 6:12, ESV

The Weight of Words That Stay

Harsh, dismissive words from someone we loved carry disproportionate weight. Our brains are wired for connection, and when people closest to us use that as a point of pressure, the impact is far beyond the surface.

Emotional pain activates the same brain regions as physical pain. Which means the pain people think of as just words or just a difficult personality is actually registered by our nervous system as a genuine threat.

The result of this is a state of chronic vigilance. This is a mindset of always watching, always adjusting, and always trying to stay one step ahead of the next wave of criticism or emotional withdrawal. Society tends to label this as over-sensitivity, but in actuality, it is the natural outcome of living in an environment where safety feels unpredictable and love seems conditional.

The weight of the words spoken isn’t lifted when the relationship ends or when the person is no longer physically present. This weight travels with the survivor long after they have left and surfaces in new relationships, quiet moments, or the way they speak to themselves when no one’s around.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, ESV

How Emotional Abuse Shapes the Way You See Yourself

The most significant and lasting effect of emotional abuse is the damage that occurs to a person’s narrative. It is this running commentary they carry about who they are and what they deserve. Survivors of emotional abuse tend to have an internal voice that sounds remarkably like the person who hurt them.

Some of the effects include second-guessing decisions, apologizing compulsively, or minimizing their own experiences. Each of these actions comes from the place of not knowing the truth after living with so many lies. Christian counselors who are trained in trauma and relational harm define this pattern as an internalized critic. It was placed there by someone else, but the survivor carries it as though it were their own honest assessment.

Untangling this inner voice from its connection to the God-given sense of self is one of the most important parts of emotional abuse recovery. This process becomes deeply sacred as it involves reclaiming an identity that was never the abuser’s to define. This was an identity that was present long before the relationship began, and it remains distorted by emotional abuse.

I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well. – Psalm 139:14, ESV

Finding Ground Again After the Damage Is Done

The process of healing from relational harm does not follow a clear or predictable timeline. Individuals often encounter setbacks connected to phrases that sound familiar or a wave of grief that arrives without warning. These are signs of a nervous system and spirit that are learning what safety feels like from the inside out. They do not define the individual as a failure or as permanently broken.

The most consistent feature of emotional abuse is isolation. Learning to rebuild community with trusted people and God is one of the most liberating and powerful steps toward broad restoration. Christian counselors help individuals understand that faith does not require minimizing what happened.

Experiencing recovery through honest prayer and lamenting, bringing the weight of the experience to God, are acts of courage, not weakness. Healing from this unseen abuse begins with a single decision to stop dismissing what you lived through.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. – Matthew 11:28, ESV

Conclusion

Emotional abuse can leave a mark that the eye cannot see, but the heart and body know it is present. The confusion and self-doubt are not imagined; they are not trivial. These are real injuries that deserve real care and a safe place to heal.

Scripture meets suffering honestly. The God who heals the broken heart and draws near to the crushed is not distant from the person who is still quietly trying to make sense of this unseen abuse. There is no way to rank the pain of emotional wounds beneath physical ones when it comes to what deserves to be addressed.

Individuals who have spent years having their reality questioned and their emotions managed deserve a space to name their experience, be believed, and taken seriously. This space exists, and it is not too late to take that first step toward building their original sense of self.

The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. – Isaiah 61:1, ESV

If you are an individual who’s navigating these lasting effects of emotional abuse, reaching out is the first step to gaining strength. Our reception team can help you connect with a counselor who understands and can help you navigate this journey of stepping away from the invisible abuse and walking toward healing.
